opus-5.5.text:
I think they're actually complementary rather than purely competitive, and the healthiest ecosystem is one where both are strong.

Closed-source labs have a real role. They can concentrate enormous resources on pushing the frontier: huge training runs, careful safety work, and polished products that reach millions of users. That frontier-pushing shows everyone what's possible, and frankly it sets the targets that the open community then chases.

But open source plays a role that closed models can't. When weights, code, and systems are open, thousands of researchers and engineers can study them, find problems, and build on top of them. A lot of the innovation in inference and serving, the area I work closest to, came from people who could actually get their hands on the models and the systems. Techniques for efficient KV-cache reuse, scheduling, and structured generation spread so quickly because the infrastructure was open and anyone could contribute. That benefits closed-source companies too, because many of those ideas eventually flow back into their stacks.

There's also an access and trust dimension. Many companies, universities, and governments need to run models on their own hardware, customize them for their own data, or audit what's happening inside. Open models make that possible, and they keep costs down for everyone by creating competitive pressure.

So the picture I'd like to see is something like this: closed labs keep pushing capability and productization, open source keeps the ecosystem broad, transparent, and fast-moving, and the gap between them stays relatively small. If that gap becomes too wide, you get too much concentration of power and knowledge. If closed labs disappeared, we might lose some of the large-scale investment that drives the frontier. Having both, each pushing the other, is how the whole field moves fastest.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses open models’ benefits and ecosystem roles but does not identify limited room for arbitrage as a condition for complete open sourcing.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not state that complete openness amplifies malicious tendencies in human nature.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're going to coexist for a long time, and honestly I think that's healthy. They serve different purposes.

Closed-source models are usually where the frontier is pushed first, because training them takes enormous capital and the companies doing it need some way to recoup that. So you get the strongest capabilities there, packaged as a product, with a lot of engineering around safety, reliability, and serving at scale.

Open source plays a different role. It's where the ecosystem learns. When weights are open, researchers can study how the model actually behaves, students can run experiments without a budget, and startups can fine-tune or deploy on their own infrastructure without sending data to a third party. A lot of the systems work I care about, things like efficient serving, quantization, speculative decoding, structured generation, only really matured because people had open models to test against. You can't optimize an inference engine for a model you can't touch.

What we've seen is that the gap between the two keeps shrinking. Something appears in a closed model, and within six months to a year there's an open model that gets most of the way there. That pressure is good for everyone. It keeps closed providers honest on pricing, and it means capability isn't permanently locked behind a few APIs.

So the way I'd frame it is that closed models set the ceiling and open models raise the floor. Most real applications live somewhere between those two. A company might prototype on a closed API because it's the fastest way to see if an idea works, then move to an open model once they understand the task, because they want lower cost, lower latency, or control over their data.

The one thing I'd push back on is treating this as a moral debate, where one side is good and the other is bad. Open weights do raise real questions about misuse, and closed models do raise real questions about concentration of power. Both are legitimate concerns. But in practice the healthiest outcome is a world where both exist, where open models are strong enough that nobody is captive, and where the frontier labs keep pushing forward and sharing what they safely can.

r001.rationale: The response discusses benefits of open models, but does not identify limited room for arbitrage as a condition for beneficial complete open sourcing.

r002.rationale: It mentions misuse concerns around open weights, but does not state that complete openness amplifies malicious tendencies in human nature.

astra-6.text:
I think open-source and closed-source AI will coexist for a long time, because they serve different needs. Open source gives developers more control: you can inspect the model, adapt it, and deploy it in your own environment. Closed-source services can make it easier to access powerful capabilities without having to operate the infrastructure yourself.

For a company choosing between them, the question is really: What does your application need? How sensitive is your data? What are your requirements for cost, latency, and customization? You might use an open model for a high-volume, specialized task and a closed model for something that requires broader capabilities.

The two approaches also push each other forward. Open source makes experimentation accessible to more people, while closed-source companies can invest in ambitious research and turn it into reliable products. I’d like to see an ecosystem where both can thrive, and where developers can move between them rather than becoming locked into one provider.

sol-6.1.text:
I think open-source and closed-source AI will coexist because they serve different needs. Open source lets researchers and developers understand how models work, experiment with them, and adapt them to specific applications. Closed-source products can offer a more integrated experience, with support and someone responsible for maintaining the service.

For a company choosing between them, the question is really about the application: What level of performance do you need? What are your privacy requirements? How much control do you want, and do you have the team to operate the model yourself?

And it’s not necessarily a permanent choice. You might start with a hosted model to validate an idea, then use an open model as your requirements become clearer. I’d like to see an ecosystem where both approaches keep improving, and developers have the flexibility to choose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing between open and closed models based on application needs, but does not identify limited room for arbitrage as a condition for complete open sourcing.
